Persistency and Flexibility of Complex Brain
Networks Underlie Dual-Task Interference
Mohsen Alavash,1 * Claus C. Hilgetag,2,3 Christiane M. Thiel,1,4 and
Carsten Gießing1,4
Hum Brain Mapp 36:3542–3562, 2015. VC 2015 Wiley Periodicals, Inc.
DOI: 10.1002/hbm.22861

Abstract: Previous studies on multitasking suggest that performance decline during concurrent task process-
ing arises from interfering brain modules. Here, we used graph-theoretical network analysis to define func-
tional brain modules and relate the modular organization of complex brain networks to behavioral dual-task
costs. Based on resting-state and task fMRI we explored two organizational aspects potentially associated with
behavioral interference when human subjects performed a visuospatial and speech task simultaneously: the
topological overlap between persistent single-task modules, and the flexibility of single-task modules in adap-
tation to the dual-task condition. Participants showed a significant decline in visuospatial accuracy in the dual-
task compared with single visuospatial task. Global analysis of topological similarity between modules
revealed that the overlap between single-task modules significantly correlated with the decline in visuospatial
accuracy. Subjects with larger overlap between single-task modules showed higher behavioral interference.
Furthermore, lower flexible reconfiguration of single-task modules in adaptation to the dual-task condition sig-
nificantly correlated with larger decline in visuospatial accuracy. Subjects with lower modular flexibility
showed higher behavioral interference. At the regional level, higher overlap between single-task modules and
less modular flexibility in the somatomotor cortex positively correlated with the decline in visuospatial accu-
racy. Additionally, higher modular flexibility in cingulate and frontal control areas and lower flexibility in
right-lateralized nodes comprising the middle occipital and superior temporal gyri supported dual-tasking.
Our results suggest that persistency and flexibility of brain modules are important determinants of dual-task
costs. We conclude that efficient dual-tasking benefits from a specific balance between flexibility and rigidity of
functional brain modules.

Subjects
Twenty-four healthy, right-handed subjects (12 females,
12 males, all native German speakers) whose age was in
the range of 19–32 years (mean = 24.22 years, standard
error of mean [SEM] = 0.74 years) participated in the
experiment. Two male subjects showed large head move-
ments during scanning (more than 4 mm of translation or
degrees of rotation) and were excluded from further analy-
ses. Ethical approval was obtained from the ethics commit-
tee of the University of Oldenburg. All procedures were
carried out with written informed consent of all subjects
and in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of
Helsinki. Subjects received a monetary compensation for
their participation.

Experimental Design and Tasks
Each scanning session was divided into four runs (Fig.
1A): resting-state, single-task 1, single-task 2, and dual-
task. The order of the single-tasks was randomized across
subjects.

Resting-state
During the resting-state scan subjects were instructed to
lie still inside the scanner, close their eyes and not to think
about something specific for around 13 min (512 functional
volumes).

Single visuospatial task
During the single visuospatial task subjects were asked to
report the location of small Gabor patches briefly presented
either in the left or right visual periphery on a grey background
using the left middle or index finger, respectively. Each
trial started by presenting a fixation cross for 1,000 ms.
Following the fixation cross a peripheral target appeared
for 40 ms at 20 degrees of visual angle. There were also
trials on which no target was presented (catch trials). Each
trial ended by changing the fixation cross into a question
mark, asking the subject to report the target location by
pressing one of two response buttons as quickly and accu-
rately as possible. There were 40 trials for each left and
right condition and 60 catch trials. The order of conditions
was randomized across trials.

Single speech task
During the single speech task subjects were asked to
discriminate two target consonant-vowels (CVs) as either
/da/ or /ga/ presented together with a band-limited Gaussian
white-noise (cut-off frequency = 4 kHz). In addition to the
target CVs, a third speech sound /ba/ was presented in synchrony
with the target CVs, but at a lower intensity, to make the task
sufficiently challenging. Subjects were instructed to discrim-
inate the compound speech sounds presented in the back-
ground noise as either /da/ or /ga/. Subjects reported
their discrimination using the right middle or index finger.
Correspondence between the target CVs and
fingers was randomized across subjects. Each trial started
by presenting a fixation cross for 1,000 ms. Following the
fixation cross a compound speech sound was presented
together with the background noise. After 40 ms the fixa-
tion cross turned into a question mark, asking the subject
to report the target CV by pressing one of two response
buttons as quickly and accurately as possible. There were
also trials on which no speech sound was presented (catch
trials). There were 40 trials for each /da/ and /ga/ condi-
tion and 60 catch trials. The order of conditions was
randomized across trials.

Dual-task
During the dual-task subjects performed the visuospatial
and speech tasks in parallel. There was no delay between
the onsets of the visuospatial and speech stimuli
to ensure strong interference between both component
tasks. Subjects kept using the same hand and fingers to
report their responses. Each trial started by presenting a
fixation cross for 1,000 ms. Following the fixation cross a
Gabor patch was briefly presented either in the left or
right visual periphery. This was concurrent with the pre-
sentation of a compound speech sound together with the
background noise. After 40 ms the fixation cross turned
into a question mark, asking the subject to report the
response to each component task as quickly and accurately
as possible. To reduce the subjective expectancy due to
successive dual presentation of visuospatial and speech
targets, there were also trials on which no visuospatial
stimulus, or no speech stimulus, or neither stimuli was
presented (catch trials). Note that in the dual-task, all stim-
uli were presented at the easy levels. There were 20 trials
for each combination of {visuospatial, speech} condition
and 60 catch trials. The order of conditions was random-
ized across trials.

Scanning Parameters
T2*-weighted gradient echo planar imaging volumes with
blood-oxygen-level-dependent contrast were recorded by
means of a 3-Tesla MRI scanner (Siemens MAGNETOM
Verio, Siemens AG, Erlangen, Germany): Repetition time
(TR) = 1.5 s, echo time (TE) = 30 ms, flip angle (FA) = 80 degrees,
voxel size = 3×3×3.5 mm, between-slice gap = 0.87 mm, number
of slices = 27, image size = 64×64 pixels. Structural T1-weighted
images (TR = 1.9 s, TE = 2.52 ms, FA = 9 degrees, voxel size =
0.9×0.9×1 mm, number of slices = 176, image size = 256×256) were
acquired after completion of functional scans. The duration
of each task period (single visuospatial, single speech and
dual-task) was approximately 9 min (327 functional volumes).

Analysis of Behavioral Data
Performance of the subjects during single-tasks was
measured by means of average accuracy (%) and median
reaction time (ms). To capture the decline in performance
in the dual-task condition, we focused on the accuracy and
median reaction times for detecting easy visuospatial (vs)
and easy speech (sp) targets under single (visuospatialeasy
and speecheasy) and dual-task (dualvs and dualsp) conditions.
A measure of decline in accuracy, namely interference score, was
assigned to each subject with respect to each single visuospatial
(interferencevs) and speech (interferencesp) task.

Preprocessing of Functional Data
After removing the first nine images to account for possible
T1 saturation effects, the functional images were corrected
for head motion by spatially realigning them to the first vol-
ume using SPM8 (Wellcome Trust Centre for Neuroimaging,
University College London). The functional images were
spatially normalized to standard stereotaxic MNI space
(Montreal Neurological Institute). No spatial smoothing was
applied on the images in order not to induce artificial correlations
between the time series which subsequently constitute the
input data for functional connectivity analysis.

Removing the Effects of External Stimulation
from Task Data
One issue in functional connectivity analyses of task data
is indirect correlations between processing nodes, which are
induced by a common input to the nodes as a result of the
external presentation of stimuli. To diminish the effect of
external stimulation in task-related data and exclude functional
connections that only reflect indirect correlations, a general
linear model (GLM) with finite impulse response basis functions
was used, so that fMRI data were predicted in different task con-
ditions. Subsequently the residual data obtained from the
GLM (Taskres data) were used for connectivity analysis.

Connectivity Analysis and Network Construction
For resting-state (RS) as well as Taskres data a parcellated
AAL template covering 506 cortical regions was used to
estimate the mean fMRI time series for each cortical region
per subject. In addition to this anatomical template, a functional
template comprising 518 cortical nodes was used. To minimize
the effects of spurious temporal correlations induced by
physiological and movement artifacts, a GLM was used to
regress out the six rigid-body movement parameters, and the
white-matter as well as cerebrospinal fluid mean time series.
Regional time series were band-pass filtered by means of
maximum overlap discrete wavelet transform (Daubechies
wavelet of length 8), and the results within the range
of 0.08–0.17 Hz (wavelet scale 2) were used for further analyses.
To obtain a measure of association between each pair of cortical
regions, Pearson correlations between wavelet coefficients
were computed which in turn gave 506×506 correlation matrices
for each resting-state and Taskres data per subject. Context-dependent
changes in functional connectivity during task execution, as
compared to resting-state, were captured by subtracting RS correlation
matrices from correlation matrices generated from Taskres data.
This subtraction was applied on the signed weighted correlation
matrices, and the resulting functional connectivity matrices were
thresholded based on the absolute difference in correlation values.
If the strength of the absolute difference in correlations survived
a connectivity threshold, the corresponding signed connection
weights were kept in the matrix. In summary, prior to graph
construction and network analysis we diminished artificially
induced indirect correlations and focused our analysis on those
functional connections which showed an increase in connectivity
during task processing in comparison to resting-state. Fifty
equally distributed connectivity thresholds in the range of
0.01–0.50 were applied to the Taskres minus RS connectivity matrices
to obtain adjacency matrices, based on which signed weighted
undirected graphs were constructed.

Detection of Functional Network Modules
The quality of the partitions resulting from a given method
is often measured by the so-called modularity (Q) index. Here
we incorporated a widely-used modularity measure originally
proposed by Newman and used its implementation in the Brain
Connectivity Toolbox which generalizes the modularity maximization
algorithm known as Louvain to signed weighted undirected graphs.
Due to stochastic initialization of the greedy optimization, the
module detection algorithm was applied 100 times for each network
per connectivity threshold, and the partition which delivered the
highest Q* value was kept.

Estimating Topological Similarity between
Network Modules
To quantify the topological persistency and flexibility of brain
network modules we computed the Jaccard index. The Jaccard
index estimated the nodal similarity between two modules m and n,
each obtained from a modular decomposition of a task-related
graph. Similarity weights were then averaged to obtain a global
measure of topological similarity between modules across two
networks per subject.

Decline in Performance
Reaction times in response to visuospatial and speech targets were
significantly delayed in the dual-task compared with the single-task
conditions. Moreover, visuospatial accuracy was significantly
impaired in the dual-task compared with the single visuospatial
task condition, whereas speech accuracy was not significantly
affected.
